messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 38-year-old hairdresser who has been single since his diagnosis with a life-threatening illness two years ago. The event began with a persistent cough and chest pain he dismissed as stress, until a routine X-ray revealed a large mass in his left lung. The weeks that followed were a blur of biopsies, CT scans, and consultations, culminating in surgery and months of chemotherapy. What stayed with him most vividly was not the diagnosis itself but the moment during a bronchoscopy when he felt the scope scrape against his ribs—a sharp, internal pressure that left him gasping. He can still smell the antiseptic and latex from that room, a chemical tang that rises unbidden when he least expects it. Sometimes, without warning, he feels that same dull ache in his ribs, even though the scans are now clear. And on his worst days, he is flooded with the full, crushing terror of those first moments after waking from surgery—the helplessness, the certainty that his body had betrayed him—without any clear image attached, just the raw emotion.

Amir works in a busy salon, a job he once loved for its social energy. But now, the environment is a minefield. When a client shows him a photo of a recent vacation, his chest tightens and his hands begin to shake. The sight of a medical ID bracelet on a customer’s wrist sends a jolt of adrenaline through him, his body going rigid as if bracing for an injection. He has started avoiding the salon’s break room because a colleague left a magazine open to an article about lung cancer; the headline alone made him feel faint. He has come to believe that his body is fundamentally unreliable, a traitor that turned against him without warning. This belief has taken root so deeply that every twinge, every minor ache, feels like a verdict. He is certain he is going crazy—that his constant vigilance, his inability to shake the feeling of doom, means something is seriously wrong with him. Because his body feels like an enemy, he scans it constantly, which only makes him more aware of every sensation, which in turn confirms that danger is imminent.

These negative appraisals have begun to generate their own triggers. His fear of going crazy makes him hypervigilant for any sign of losing control, so the sudden memory of the smell of antiseptic can send him into a spiral of panic, which he then interprets as proof that he is, in fact, losing his mind. The memory of the pain in his ribs can be triggered not only by a medical setting but also by the mere thought that his body might be failing him again. And once that memory arrives, it amplifies his sense of threat, making his muscles tense and his breathing shallow, which in turn primes his body to recall the physical sensations of the illness. The cycle is relentless: a trigger—a photo, a scent, a routine physical exam—pulls him into the memory, which confirms his appraisal of his body as untrustworthy, which heightens his threat response, which makes him more sensitive to the next trigger.

He recently had to cancel a haircut appointment for a long-time client because the salon’s receptionist mentioned she had just returned from a hospital visit. The word alone made his stomach drop. He called in sick, spending the day in his apartment, hyperaware of his own heartbeat. What finally brought him to seek help was a nightmare so vivid he woke up tasting the rubber of the breathing tube, convinced he was back in the ICU. He lay in the dark for hours, too afraid to close his eyes, certain that if he fell asleep his body would stop breathing again. He is terrified that he will never feel safe in his own skin, that his life will shrink to the size of his fear. But he is also, for the first time, hoping that someone can show him a way out of the loop.
